k: What this is This is a complete set of topic guides for Pearson Edexcel A Level Mathematics (9MA0) — the whole two-year course, Year 12 and Year 13, Pure, Statistics and Mechanics. Every topic guide follows the same shape: 1. Why this topic exists — what problem it solves, and where it plugs into the rest of the course. 2. The ideas, built up in order — each new bit of machinery explained from the ground up, with the reasoning shown, not just the rule stated. 3. Worked examples — full solutions with the thinking written out, including the choices you have to make and why you make them. 4. Common mistakes — the specific, predictable ways students drop marks on this topic. 5. In the exam — what questions actually look like, what examiners want to see written down. 6. Practice questions — graded from routine to exam-standard, each with a full worked solution behind a toggle. How to actually use it (read this bit) Here is the uncomfortable truth about maths revision: reading a worked solution feels like learning and mostly isn't. When you read someone else's solution, your brain goes "yes, obviously, I could have done that." That feeling is called fluency illusion and it is the single biggest reason people walk out of a maths exam surprised by their own grade. So the rule for every practice question on this site: Attempt the question on paper, fully, to an answer , before you open the solution. If you get stuck, note exactly where you got stuck, then open the solution and read only until you're unstuck. Close it. Finish the question yourself. A workable routine for one topic: 1. Read the explanation sections properly once. Slowly. Pen in hand. 2. Cover each worked example's solution and try it first. Then compare, line by line. 3. Do the practice questions cold, on paper, timed roughly at 1.2 minutes per mark. 4. Mark yourself honestly against the solution. Write down every mark you dropped and why . 5. Come back to that topic 3 days later and redo the two questions you got wrong. This is the step everyone skips and it's the step that does the work. The four things that actually raise a maths grade - Spacing. Revisiting a topic after a gap beats re-reading it now. A topic done once and revisited three times over a term will outperform a topic hammered for four hours in one sitting. - Retrieval. k: The three papers Edexcel A Level Mathematics (9MA0) is assessed by three papers, all sat at the end of Year 13. There is no coursework and no non-calculator paper — a calculator is allowed in all three . Paper Content Length Marks Weight --- --- --- --- --- Paper 1: Pure Mathematics 1 Any pure topic from either year 2 hours 100 33⅓% Paper 2: Pure Mathematics 2 Any pure topic from either year 2 hours 100 33⅓% Paper 3: Statistics and Mechanics Section A: Statistics (50 marks)<br Section B: Mechanics (50 marks) 2 hours 100 33⅓% Two consequences that people underestimate: - Pure is two-thirds of the qualification. If you are short on time, pure is where the marks are. - Papers 1 and 2 are not split by year or by topic. Either paper can ask anything from the pure content. There is no "Paper 1 is Year 12". Everything is examinable everywhere. The grade boundaries typically land somewhere around 55–65% for an A, and around 80% for an A (the A is awarded on the overall total, not on a specific paper). Those move year to year — treat them as a rough map, not a target. Timing 200 marks of pure in 240 minutes, so 1.2 minutes per mark . A 6-mark question deserves about 7 minutes. If you're 3 minutes over on a question, leave it, mark it, come back. Students lose far more marks to unfinished papers than to wrong answers. What's in Year 12 vs Year 13 The split below is the standard Edexcel teaching order. The specification itself doesn't formally split AS from A2 content in the A Level, but this is how virtually every school sequences it, and it's how this resource is organised. Why this topic exists The gradient of a straight line is easy: rise over run, and it's the same everywhere. A curve's gradient changes from point to point. Differentiation is the machinery for finding it — a function that tells you the gradient at any you like. That one idea answers an enormous range of questions: where is this curve steepest, where does it turn, what's the maximum profit, what's the velocity at time , what shape of can uses least metal. Calculus is the single most useful thing in A Level maths, and roughly a quarter of the pure marks depend on it. --- 1. The idea: gradient as a limit Take a curve and two points on it, and . Proof by contradiction is the fourth proof technique, and it's the one that unlocks results you can't get any other way — that is irrational, that there are infinitely many primes. Partial fractions looks like pointless algebra until you meet integration in Year 13, where is impossible as written but trivial once split. It's also needed for binomial expansions of rational functions. --- 1. Proof by contradiction 1. Assume the opposite of what you want to prove. 2. Reason logically from that assumption. 3. Reach something impossible — a contradiction. 4. Conclude that the assumption must have been false, so the original statement is true. A statement is either true or false; there's no third option. If assuming it's false leads to an impossibility, then it can't be false. So it's true. That's the entire logic. The craft is in step 2 — choosing what to do with the assumption so that a contradiction actually appears.
